title: Eumaeus' farmstead
greek: αὐλὴ ... καλή τε μεγάλη τε, περίδρομος (aulē ... kalē te megalē te, peridromos); συφεοὺς δυοκαίδεκα (twelve sties)
short: The swineherd's walled yard with twelve sties of fifty sows each, described in language borrowed from Priam's palace.
body: Eumaeus has built the enclosure himself, without orders from Penelope or Laertes, out of quarried stone topped with thorn and ringed with oak stakes split to the dark heart-wood; Monro explains peridromos as an open space round it 'serving as the glacis of the fortress', rhutoisin as 'quarried' stones and to melan as the dark core of the oak. Inside are twelve sties, each holding fifty breeding sows, while the boars, thinned by the suitors' feasting, number 360. Monro observes that lines 13-16 almost parody the description of Priam's palace in Il. 6.244-50, with its fifty chambers 'close by one another' for Priam's sons, and in his Appendix he lists the passage among the Odyssey's playful uses of Iliadic language. The careful farm is a portrait of the loyal servant: he has protected and increased his absent master's property while the suitors devour it.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 14.7, 14.10, 14.12 and 14.13-16.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), Appendix II, p. 331 (Odyssean parody of Iliadic formulas).
Homer, Iliad 6.242-250 (Priam's palace).

title: Odysseus and the farm dogs
greek: κύνες ὑλακόμωροι (kunes hulakomōroi), 'baying hounds'; ἕζετο κερδοσύνῃ (hezeto kerdosunēi), 'sat down in his cunning'
short: Attacked by the swineherd's dogs, Odysseus sits down and drops his staff, a trick that calms them.
body: The four dogs, 'savage as wild beasts', are called hulakomōroi, a word LSJ glosses 'always barking'; Monro thinks it a mock-heroic coinage on the pattern of the Iliad's enchesimōroi, 'spear-mad'. Odysseus' response is practical: he sits and lets his staff fall. Plutarch, in his essay on the intelligence of animals (De sollertia animalium 15), quotes these lines as proof that dogs stop attacking those who throw themselves down in an attitude of humility. Eumaeus drives the dogs off with stones and remarks that, had his guest been mauled, he would have borne the reproach, so that the very first words of the scene concern the host's duty to protect a stranger. Dogs are a running motif in this part of the poem: they fawn on Telemachus (16.4-10), cower before Athena (16.162-3) and, most famously, the old dog Argos recognises his master (17.291-327).

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ὑλακόμωρος.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 14.29.
Plutarch, De sollertia animalium (On the Cleverness of Animals) 15, quoting Od. 14.29-31.

title: Eumaeus 'leader of men' (orchamos andrōn)
greek: ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν (orchamos andrōn)
short: A heroic title used of princes in the Iliad and here given to a slave swineherd.
body: LSJ defines orchamos as 'leader, chief'; the phrase orchamos andrōn is used of warrior leaders in the Iliad (2.837) and of Nestor's son Peisistratus (Od. 3.400), and in the Odyssey also of the loyal cowherd Philoetius (20.185, 254). Applied to Eumaeus, who does command four under-herdsmen, it is either gentle humour or a genuine mark of dignity, and readers have taken it both ways. Monro's Appendix treats several epithets in this book (the 'baying' dogs, the palace-like sties) as playful adaptations of Iliadic style, and the swineherd's title belongs with them. Yet the poem consistently treats Eumaeus with respect: he is dios huphorbos, 'the goodly swineherd', he is addressed directly by the narrator, and we later learn that he was born a king's son (15.403-14). The heroic language suits a man of noble birth and noble conduct reduced to slavery.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ὄρχαμος.
Homer, Odyssey 3.400 (Peisistratus orchamos andrōn).
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), Appendix II, p. 331.

anchor: swineherd Eumaeus, didst thou make answer
title: The narrator's address to Eumaeus
greek: τὸν δ' ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα (ton d' apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie subōta)
short: Homer's narrator turns and speaks to Eumaeus as 'you', something he does with no other character in the Odyssey.
body: This is the first of fifteen places in the Odyssey where the narrator introduces Eumaeus' speech with a second-person verb, prosephēs, 'you answered' (five times in Book 14 alone). The Iliad does something similar for Patroclus and Menelaus. Scholars disagree about why. One explanation is metrical: the vocative Eumaie subōta fills the end of the line conveniently. Others see an expression of affection or sympathy, an intimacy between poet and character; Elizabeth Block, 'The Narrator Speaks: Apostrophe in Homer and Vergil', TAPA 112 (1982) 7-22, discusses the device in both poets. Whatever its origin, the effect for a reader is to single out the swineherd as one of the poem's most sympathetic figures. His name is first given here; ancient and modern guesses at its meaning (for example 'good seeker') remain uncertain.

sources.cite: E. Block, 'The Narrator Speaks: Apostrophe in Homer and Vergil', Transactions of the American Philological Association 112 (1982) 7-22.
Homer, Odyssey 14.55.
Homer, Odyssey 16.60 (the same address in Book 16).

anchor: this is the lot of slaves
title: Eumaeus' hospitality and the lot of slaves
greek: πρὸς γὰρ Διός εἰσιν ἅπαντες ξεῖνοί τε πτωχοί τε· δόσις δ' ὀλίγη τε φίλη τε (dosis d' oligē te philē te); ἡ γὰρ δμώων δίκη ἐστίν
short: Eumaeus explains that strangers come from Zeus, that his gift is small, and that slaves live in fear of young masters.
body: Eumaeus repeats Nausicaa's principle that 'all strangers and beggars are from Zeus' (6.207-8), but adds his own social reality. Monro notes that 'a gift, small and kindly' is a set phrase that Eumaeus uses as a euphemism to soften what he means, that his means are small, and paraphrases 'that is the manner of bondsmen', namely to be cautious and sparing. The 'young masters' (hoi neoi) are the suitors, who now rule the household. Eumaeus' speech reveals the hope of a faithful slave: a good master would have given him a house, land and a wife (14.62-7). The scene is the Odyssey's fullest picture of xenia practised by the poor, and it is the positive pattern against which the suitors' abuse of the stranger in Books 17-20 will be measured.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 14.58, 14.59 and 14.61.
Homer, Odyssey 6.207-208 (Nausicaa on strangers and beggars).
Homer, Odyssey 14.56-67.

anchor: loosened the knees of many warriors
title: Helen 'loosed the knees' of many men
greek: ὡς ὤφελλ' Ἑλένης ἀπὸ φῦλον ὀλέσθαι πρόχνυ, ἐπεὶ πολλῶν ἀνδρῶν ὑπὸ γούνατ' ἔλυσε (prochnu ... gounat' eluse)
short: Eumaeus curses Helen's race, using the Iliadic idiom for killing a man, 'loosening his knees'.
body: To 'loosen the knees' is a regular Iliadic expression for killing, from the collapse of a man struck down. Eumaeus wishes that Helen's whole kin had perished prochnu, literally 'onto the knees', a word used figuratively of utter ruin; Monro points out the pun: 'may the race of Helen fall and be brought to its knees, even as she has loosed the knees of many men'. The same formula describes the 'hateful journey' to Troy in Odysseus' Cretan tale (14.235-6). The curse places the swineherd's private loss within the larger catastrophe of the Trojan War: his master went to Troy 'to win recompense for Agamemnon' (14.70-1) and, as far as Eumaeus knows, never came back.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 14.69.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. γόνυ.
Homer, Odyssey 14.235-236 (the same formula).

title: Opis: the gods' watchful regard
greek: οὐκ ὄπιδα φρονέοντες ἐνὶ φρεσὶν οὐδ' ἐλεητύν (ouk opida phroneontes eni phresin oud' eleētun)
short: Murray's 'wrath of the gods' renders opis, the gods' watch over human wrongdoing and the punishment that follows.
body: LSJ explains opis as the 'vengeance or visitation of the gods for transgressing divine laws', always in a bad sense in Homer; Monro calls it 'the regard of the gods', their watch kept on human transgression. Eumaeus' little sermon (14.80-92) gives the poem's moral argument in the mouth of a slave: the gods 'love not reckless deeds, but honor justice', and even pirates feel fear of opis once they have their plunder. The suitors, by contrast, behave as if they knew Odysseus to be dead and themselves safe from consequences. This echoes Zeus' complaint in the opening council that mortals blame the gods for evils they bring on themselves by recklessness (1.32-43), and it prepares the reader to view the coming slaughter as divine justice rather than mere revenge.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ὄπις.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 14.82.
Homer, Odyssey 1.32-43 (Zeus on human recklessness).

title: Odysseus' herds
greek: δώδεκ' ἐν ἠπείρῳ ἀγέλαι (dōdek' en ēpeirōi agelai)
short: Eumaeus lists Odysseus' wealth in livestock, on the mainland and on Ithaca, now being eaten by the suitors.
body: Heroic wealth was measured largely in animals. Odysseus owns twelve herds of cattle, twelve flocks of sheep, twelve droves of pigs and twelve herds of goats on the mainland opposite Ithaca, tended by his own men and by hired foreigners, as well as eleven herds of goats on the island itself, besides Eumaeus' pigs. Eumaeus claims that not twenty men together are as rich. The point is not idle: every day each herdsman must send his best animal to the palace for the suitors (14.105-8), so the catalogue measures the scale of the household's ruin, a theme Telemachus stated in the assembly of Book 2. Monro notes that suboisia (14.101) is lengthened by metrical licence and that ep-orontai means 'are watchers over them'.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 14.101 and 14.104.
Homer, Odyssey 14.96-108.
Homer, Odyssey 2.55-59 (Telemachus on the suitors' consumption).

anchor: a reward for bearing good tidings
title: Euangelion: reward for good news
greek: εὐαγγέλιον δέ μοι ἔστω (euangelion de moi estō)
short: The Greek word for a messenger's reward for good news, later the word translated 'gospel'.
body: LSJ defines euangelion as the 'reward of good tidings, given to the messenger', citing these two lines as its first appearances in Greek. Odysseus asks for a cloak and tunic as his reward, but only when Odysseus has actually returned; until then he refuses to accept anything, because he hates the beggar who lies for gain. Eumaeus replies that he will never pay it (14.166). The custom is ancient and widespread: in 2 Samuel 4:10 David recalls a messenger who expected 'a reward for his tidings', where the Greek Septuagint uses the same word. In later Greek the word came to mean the good news itself, and in the New Testament it names the Christian message, translated into English as 'gospel', so this exchange in a pig-farm contains the earliest occurrence of a word with a long history.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. εὐαγγέλιον.
2 Samuel 4:10 (King James Version).
Homer, Odyssey 14.152-166.

title: 'Hateful as the gates of Hades'
greek: ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς Ἀΐδαο πύλῃσι (echthros gar moi keinos homōs Aïdao pulēisi)
short: Odysseus borrows the line Achilles once used against him in the Iliad, about the man who says one thing and thinks another.
body: In the Embassy of Iliad 9, Achilles answers Odysseus' persuasive speech by saying that he hates 'as the gates of Hades' the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another (Il. 9.312-13). Here Odysseus, in disguise and about to tell a long false tale, applies the same formula to the beggar who lies for the sake of a cloak. Whether or not the poet intended a pointed allusion, the irony for anyone who knows the Iliad is striking: the man Achilles suspected of duplicity now uses Achilles' own words to vouch for his honesty. The formula belongs to the language of oaths and strong denials; Odysseus follows it with a solemn oath on Zeus, the table and the hearth (14.158-9).

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 9.312-313 (Achilles to Odysseus).
Homer, Odyssey 14.156-157.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. πύλη.

title: Oath by the table and the hearth
greek: ἴστω νῦν Ζεὺς πρῶτα θεῶν ξενίη τε τράπεζα ἱστίη τ' Ὀδυσῆος (istō nun Zeus prōta theōn xeniē te trapeza histiē t' Odusēos)
short: Odysseus swears by Zeus, the guest-table and Odysseus' own hearth that Odysseus will return; Eumaeus refuses the oath.
body: Monro notes that in Homer the hearth (histiē) is a sacred object, but not yet the goddess Hestia of later religion, and that the word occurs only in this oath formula, the ordinary word for hearth being eschara; strictly the 'hearth of Odysseus' belongs to the palace, not the hut. LSJ likewise notes that Homer uses histiē only in solemn appeals. The same oath, almost word for word, is sworn to Penelope in 19.303-7, and Monro argues that the precise lines fixing the day (14.161-2) belong more naturally there. By swearing on the table of hospitality the stranger binds himself by the very relationship he enjoys with Eumaeus, which makes the oath more solemn and, given that he is Odysseus, literally true. Eumaeus declines to take it seriously, saying 'we will let it be' (14.171).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 14.158-162 and 14.159.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἑστία.
Homer, Odyssey 19.303-307 (the same oath to Penelope).

title: Lukabas: 'this very day' or 'this very year'?
greek: τοῦδ' αὐτοῦ λυκάβαντος ἐλεύσεται (toud' autou lukabantos eleusetai); τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνός, τοῦ δ' ἱσταμένοιο
short: A rare word whose meaning was disputed: most authorities say 'year', but Monro (followed by Murray) argues for 'day'.
body: LSJ translates lukabas as 'year' ('within this very year'), adds that Dio Chrysostom took it as 'month', and notes that it might mean 'day' if these lines are not genuine. Monro argued at length that the word, explained in antiquity as 'the path of light', should mean a day, a full cycle of night and day, and that 'as the old moon wanes and the new appears' points to the day the Athenians called 'old and new', the last day of one month and the first of the next. That day is the feast of Apollo on which the suitors die (20.156, 21.258). A promise 'within the year' would sound like mockery to a Penelope on the verge of remarriage, whereas 'this very day' is exactly fulfilled in Book 19. Murray's 'in the course of this self-same day' agrees with Monro's interpretation; most other translators keep 'year'. The 'moonless' night at 14.457 fits the same calendar.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. λυκάβας.
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 14.158-162 (on λυκάβας and the new moon).
Homer, Odyssey 19.306-307 (the same prophecy to Penelope).

title: The second Cretan tale: 'Castor son of Hylax'
greek: Κάστωρ Ὑλακίδης (Kastōr Hulakidēs)
short: Odysseus' invented Cretan father, whose name suggests 'Barker'; the hero casts himself as a bastard son cheated of his inheritance.
body: In his longest false tale (14.192-359) Odysseus becomes the son of a rich Cretan, Castor, by a bought concubine. On the father's death the legitimate sons divide the estate by lot and give him a pittance, and he makes his fortune by marriage and raiding. The father's name Hulakidēs looks as if it comes from hulaō, 'to bark' (compare hulakē, 'barking', in LSJ, and the 'baying' dogs of 14.29), a joke at the expense of a fictitious pedigree, though Homer does not comment on it. Monro notes that 'cast lots for it' describes dividing an estate and assigning shares by lot, the normal procedure among heirs. The story's details, a man of ability excluded from wealth who wins honour by his spear, make an ideal appeal to a sympathetic slave who also knows what it is to have lost his birthright.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 14.209 and 14.210.
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ὑλακή.
Homer, Odyssey 14.199-210.

title: The stubble and the grain
greek: καλάμην γέ σ' ὀΐομαι εἰσορόωντα γιγνώσκειν (kalamēn ge s' oïomai eisoroōnta gignōskein)
short: The beggar asks Eumaeus to judge the harvest of his youth from the stubble of his old age.
body: Kalamē is the stalk or stubble left after reaping. LSJ lists this line as the example of its metaphorical use 'of an old man'. Aristotle, discussing metaphor in the Rhetoric (3.10, 1410b), quotes the image as an example of a metaphor that teaches us something, because calling old age 'stubble' brings out what old age and stubble share: both have lost their bloom. The phrase is typical of the Cretan tale's rhetoric, which asks Eumaeus to read a shabby exterior as evidence of a distinguished past, exactly what the whole disguise requires of those who meet Odysseus in Ithaca.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. καλάμη.
Aristotle, Rhetoric 3.10, 1410b13-15 (old age as 'stubble').
Homer, Odyssey 14.214-215.

title: The raider's temperament
greek: ἄλλος γάρ τ' ἄλλοισιν ἀνὴρ ἐπιτέρπεται ἔργοις (allos gar t' alloisin anēr epiterpetai ergois)
short: The 'Cretan' prefers ships, war and raiding to farming and family, and grew rich on nine raids before Troy.
body: The invented Cretan confesses that work on the land and the care of a household never pleased him; he loved oared ships, wars, polished spears and arrows, 'grievous things' that make others shudder. He led nine raids against foreigners, choosing his share of the plunder before the rest was distributed by lot (Monro on 14.232 explains the division of spoil after the leader's special prizes). The self-portrait mirrors the real Odysseus, who sacked Ismarus on the way home from Troy (9.39-61) and calls himself 'sacker of cities'. Monro regards the gnomic line 14.228, 'different men take joy in different works', as a later addition, partly because the form ergois is post-Homeric. The speech is a reminder that the hero's world rested on predatory raiding, as natural to Homeric society as farming.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 14.228 and 14.232.
Homer, Odyssey 9.39-61 (the raid on the Cicones).
Homer, Odyssey 14.222-234.

title: The raid on Egypt
greek: πεμπταῖοι δ' Αἴγυπτον ἐϋρρείτην ἱκόμεσθα (pemptaioi d' Aigupton eurreitēn hikometha)
short: The false Cretan's failed raid on the Nile, his surrender to the Egyptian king and seven years of wealth in Egypt.
body: Aiguptos in Homer is the name of the river (the Nile) as well as the land, as Monro notes. The crew disobey orders, plunder the fields and carry off women and children; at dawn the Egyptians counter-attack with chariots and the raiders are killed or enslaved. The narrator saves himself by throwing down his arms and clasping the king's knees, and the king protects him out of fear of 'Zeus the stranger's god'. Monro points out that the seven years of prosperity in Egypt replace the seven years Odysseus really spent with Calypso. The same story is retold to Antinous (17.424-44). Historians have compared it with the attacks of the 'Sea Peoples' on the Nile Delta recorded by pharaohs of the thirteenth and twelfth centuries BC; Jeffrey P. Emanuel argues for close parallels with the Sherden mercenaries, while stressing that the tale is fiction within the poem.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 14.246 and 14.285.
Homer, Odyssey 17.424-444 (the tale retold).

J. P. Emanuel, 'Cretan Lie and Historical Truth: Examining Odysseus' Raid on Egypt in its Late Bronze Age Context' (Center for Hellenic Studies); see also his Black Ships and Sea Raiders (Lanham: Lexington Books).

title: The course past Crete
greek: μέσσον ὑπὲρ Κρήτης (messon huper Krētēs)
short: The Phoenician's ship, bound for Libya, runs before the north wind past Crete before Zeus wrecks it with a thunderbolt.
body: Monro gives a seaman's reading of the route. The ship sails from Phoenicia towards Libya and must pass Crete; huper here does not mean 'beyond' but, as at 3.170, indicates the side on which the ship passed, the north-west or windward side, keeping clear of the lee shore. The alternative course, along the south coast under the lee of the island, was the one taken by St Paul's ship (Acts 27:7). After the wreck the survivor drifts nine days to Thesprotia; Monro quotes J. L. Myres that the main current of the Mediterranean regularly sets from Crete towards that coast, though he still thinks the distance improbable. The storm sequence (black cloud, thunderbolt, smell of sulphur, crew in the sea like sea-crows, the hero clinging to the mast) repeats Odysseus' real shipwreck after Thrinacia (12.403-25), another true detail recycled in the lie.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 14.300 and 14.315.
Acts 27:7 (King James Version).
Homer, Odyssey 12.403-425 (the real shipwreck).

title: Thesprotia and king Pheidon
greek: γαίῃ Θεσπρωτῶν (gaiēi Thesprōtōn); ἐκομίσσατο Φείδων ἥρως ἀπριάτην (ekomissato Pheidōn hērōs apriatēn)
short: A region of Epirus on the mainland north of Ithaca, where the invented king Pheidon received the castaway without ransom.
body: Thesprotia lay in Epirus, on the coast opposite Corcyra, near the oracle of Dodona and the river Acheron. Pheidon takes the castaway in apriatēn, 'without purchase-money', the same word used in the Iliad of Chryseis, returned to her father 'without price or ransom' (Il. 1.99; LSJ). The kindly king claims to have entertained Odysseus himself and shows his treasures, a detail that lets the disguised hero report his own survival and wealth. Thesprotia recurs in the poem: Antinous' father once raided the Thesprotians, Ithaca's allies (16.426-7), and according to Proclus' summary of the post-Homeric Telegony, Odysseus himself later went there and married its queen Callidice. Monro notes that the name Thesprotia first appears in the Odyssey, as a land on the westward route from Greece. The crew of the Thesprotian ship who try to sell the stranger as a slave provide his explanation for arriving on Ithaca in rags.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἀπριάτην.
Homer, Iliad 1.99 (Chryseis returned without ransom).
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), Appendix II, p. 337 (Thesprotia first named in the Odyssey) and Appendix III, p. 382 (Proclus' summary of the Telegony).

title: The oracle of Zeus at Dodona
greek: ἐς Δωδώνην ... ὄφρα θεοῖο ἐκ δρυὸς ὑψικόμοιο Διὸς βουλὴν ἐπακούσαι (ek druos hupsikomoio Dios boulēn epakousai)
short: Zeus' oracle in Epirus, where his will was heard from a sacred oak; Odysseus is said to have gone to consult it.
body: Dodona, in the mountains of Epirus, was the most ancient oracle of Zeus. Achilles prays to 'Zeus of Dodona' whose priests, the Selloi, 'sleep on the ground with unwashed feet' (Il. 16.233-5), and in the Odyssey the god's will is learned from the 'high-crested oak', presumably from the rustling of its leaves. Herodotus later reports the priestesses' story that the oracle was founded by a black dove from Egyptian Thebes and calls it the oldest in Greece (2.52-7). Monro observes in his Appendix that consulting local oracles is characteristic of the Odyssey (Dodona here and in Book 19, Delphi at 8.80, and the 'oracles of Zeus' at 16.403). The false report that Odysseus has gone to ask whether to return 'openly or in secret' is apt, since secrecy is exactly what he is now practising.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 16.233-235 (Zeus of Dodona and the Selloi).
Herodotus, Histories 2.52-57 (origins of Dodona).
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), Appendix II, p. 336 (local oracles in the Odyssey).

anchor: for the nymphs and for Hermes
title: Eumaeus' sacrifice and the seven portions
greek: τὴν μὲν ἴαν νύμφῃσι καὶ Ἑρμῇ, Μαιάδος υἱεῖ, θῆκεν ἐπευξάμενος (tēn men ian numphēisi kai Hermēi, Maiados huiei)
short: A rustic sacrifice in full: hair as first-offering, raw pieces in fat, and one of seven shares for the nymphs and Hermes.
body: The slaughter of a five-year-old boar follows the stages of Homeric sacrifice on a humble scale. Eumaeus throws bristles from the head into the fire as a first-offering (aparchomenos), prays for Odysseus' return, stuns the animal with a log, and after the throat is cut lays bits of raw flesh from every limb in fat and burns them sprinkled with barley meal, the gods' share. The meat is divided into seven portions, one reserved for the nymphs and Hermes, the patrons of a herdsman. Monro notes that the ritual pieces represent the gods' share of the sacrifice, while the seventh portion was kept for the host's special patrons, and quotes J. L. Myres on the modern Greek host who still carves and apportions every piece himself. In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes the infant god himself slaughters cattle and divides the meat into twelve portions by lot (lines 128-9).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 14.419, 14.428, 14.432 and 14.435.
Homeric Hymn 4, To Hermes 112-137 (Hermes divides the meat).
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἄργμα.

title: The chine as a portion of honour
greek: νώτοισιν δ' Ὀδυσῆα διηνεκέεσσι γέραιρεν (nōtoisin d' Odusēa diēnekeessi gerairen)
short: Eumaeus honours his guest with the long back-cut, the traditional mark of distinction at a Homeric meal.
body: The chine (nōta, the meat along the backbone) was the portion of honour (geras). Agamemnon gives Ajax 'the long chine' after his duel with Hector (Il. 7.321-2), Menelaus sets the chine before Telemachus (4.65-6), and Odysseus sends a cut of it to the singer Demodocus (8.474-6). Eumaeus therefore treats the ragged stranger as a hero, without knowing that he is honouring his own master, and the narrator comments that he 'made glad the heart of his master'. Monro observes that, strictly, the honour-portion would be given before the general division into shares. Odysseus' reply, wishing that Eumaeus may be as dear to Zeus as he is to him, is one of several moments in which a blessing from the disguised king carries more weight than the speaker can reveal.

sources.cite: Homer, Iliad 7.321-322 (Ajax honoured with the chine).
Homer, Odyssey 4.65-66 (Menelaus honours Telemachus).

title: Mesaulius, the slave of a slave
greek: Μεσαύλιος, ὅν ῥα συβώτης αὐτὸς κτήσατο οἶος ... πὰρ δ' ἄρα μιν Ταφίων πρίατο (Mesaulios ... par d' ara min Taphiōn priato)
short: Eumaeus' own servant, bought from Taphian traders with his savings: a slave who owns a slave.
body: The detail reveals the economic life of the household. Eumaeus, himself bought as a boy (15.483), has used his own resources to purchase an attendant from the Taphians, sea-traders and pirates whose lord Mentes Athena impersonated in Book 1, and he did it, like the building of his farm, without consulting Penelope or Laertes. Homeric slavery thus allowed a trusted slave some property of his own, which Eumaeus hopes would have been increased by a grateful master (14.62-7). The name has been connected with messaulos, the inner part of a farmyard where animals are kept at night (LSJ s.v. μέσαυλος), which would make it a 'speaking name' for a farm servant, though Homer gives no explanation. Mesaulius serves the bread and clears the meal, a small figure who completes the picture of an orderly rustic household.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. μέσαυλος.
Homer, Odyssey 14.449-455.

title: 'Befooling wine'
greek: οἶνος γὰρ ἀνώγει ἠλεός (oinos gar anōgei ēleos)
short: Odysseus blames the wine for the tale he is about to tell, a playful excuse for an indirect request.
body: LSJ explains ēleos as 'distraught, crazed' and, in its active sense here, 'crazing', with this line as the example. Odysseus describes how wine makes even a wise man sing, laugh softly, dance and 'bring forth a word which were better unspoken'. Monro notes that the verb he uses for 'spoke out' (anekragon, 14.467) has a colloquial stamp. The excuse is of course a pretence: the tale that follows is carefully constructed to hint that Eumaeus should lend him a cloak on this cold, wet night, without the indignity of asking directly. The theme of wine loosening the tongue is old in Greek poetry; in the Odyssey the opposite case is the Cyclops, whom Odysseus made drunk precisely in order to deceive (9.345-74).

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἠλεός.

Homer, Odyssey 14.462-467.

title: Ainos: a tale with a purpose
greek: ὦ γέρον, αἶνος μέν τοι ἀμύμων, ὃν κατέλεξας (ainos men toi amumōn, hon katelexas)
short: Eumaeus calls the beggar's story of the night ambush at Troy an ainos and understands its hint: he lends him a cloak.
body: The beggar tells how, lying in ambush beneath Troy on a freezing night without a cloak, he complained to Odysseus, who promptly invented a 'dream from the gods' requiring a messenger, so that Thoas son of Andraemon jumped up, threw off his purple cloak and ran to the ships, leaving the cloak for the narrator. The point is unspoken: 'I am cold now, and I have no cloak.' Eumaeus calls it an ainos, which LSJ defines as 'tale, story', especially a story with a moral or hidden purpose, a fable; Monro thinks the senses 'fable' and 'praise' are not yet clearly present in Homer. Either way, Eumaeus grasps the message, gives his guest a bed by the fire and a thick cloak for the night. Monro notes that 14.504-6 were rejected by ancient critics as spoiling the point by asking too directly. The tale also portrays Odysseus' resourcefulness through his own (invented) eyes.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. αἶνος.

Homer, Iliad 2.638-638 (Thoas son of Andraemon, leader of the Aetolians).
